title: MoQ for the Curious
text:
About this book
MoQ for the Curious explains how Media over QUIC delivers live content: how publishers name it, relays distribute it, and players keep it useful when the network slows.
We’ll introduce the networking and media concepts as we need them. To see how they fit together, we’ll follow an online lecture from the moment a student joins to the moment they hear the lecturer.
This book is inspired by WebRTC for the Curious and its approach to explaining how the pieces of a real-time communication system fit together.
Start reading: What, Why and How →

title: MoQ for the Curious
text:
Where to begin
Start with the first chapter for an introduction and a comparison with WebRTC. Continue in order to follow the lecture through networking, subscriptions, relays, and playback. If you already know the basics, use Your First MoQ System to find demos and libraries to start with. The glossary explains unfamiliar terms along the way.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
What is MoQ?
Imagine you’re building an app for a live lecture. The lecturer shares a camera and microphone, students join halfway through, and some of them have bad connections. How do we get useful audio and video to everyone?
That’s the problem we’ll use to explore MoQ. We’ll start with what it does and how it compares with WebRTC, then follow the lecture from the publisher to a student’s player.
Media over QUIC (MoQ) lets applications publish live content that other applications can subscribe to. A publisher can send content directly to subscribers or distribute it through relays. MoQ Transport (MOQT) is the protocol that defines how content is named, requested, and delivered. It runs over QUIC, a secure transport with multiple independent byte streams, either directly or through WebTransport.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
Where does WebRTC fit?
If you’ve built a video call with WebRTC, you’ve used a browser stack that handles encoding, sending, receiving, and decoding media. With MoQ, those pieces are assembled by a media library around MOQT, the protocol that delivers the content. This gives the library more choices about how to package and play it. We’ll get into the details below.
Separating those pieces gives an application more control over playback. In a conversation, you want quick responses. When watching a broadcast, you might prefer a little extra buffering if it keeps the video from stalling. The moq.dev article Replacing WebRTC discusses this tradeoff.


A lecture as an example
MoQ uses a publish/subscribe model: one endpoint makes content available, and another asks to receive it.
In our lecture, the lecturer publishes live audio, video, and slides. Students choose what to receive on their own devices.
In this example, the lecturer is a publisher. Each viewer is a subscriber. If the lecturer sent a separate 2 Mb/s copy to 100 students, their connection would need to upload 200 Mb/s. Every new student would add more work to the lecturer’s connection.
Instead, the lecturer sends one copy to a relay, a server that forwards it to the students. The lecturer uploads 2 Mb/s, while the relay handles the copies for all 100 viewers. As the audience grows, we can add relays and spread that work across servers. These numbers count media bytes, before network overhead.
For the browser setup in this book, a reachable relay is required when the lecturer and students are behind private networks. Both sides connect out to it, and it forwards the media between them. They can’t open WebTransport connections directly to each other, and MOQT doesn’t provide NAT traversal to make that possible. So we need the relay even for one lecturer and one student, before scaling becomes a concern. We’ll explain the connection setup below.


The relay receives the publication once and forwards the tracks each viewer requests. Blue is audio; purple is video. Requests and transport acknowledgments are omitted.

An endpoint can be both a publisher and a subscriber: a student can receive the lecture and publish microphone audio over the same session. A relay receives content upstream and publishes it downstream. See the draft’s role definitions.
To let the viewers make different choices, the publisher gives the pieces separate names. The lecturer’s audio can be one track, camera video another, and slides a third. A track contains individually identifiable pieces of data called objects. For example, a media format might place one compressed video frame in each object. The phone viewer requests the audio track; the laptop viewer requests audio and video.
A relay can also cache objects: keep copies so it can answer later requests. Someone joining the lecture may need content published a moment earlier to begin playback. If the relay has kept that content, it can supply it without asking the lecturer to send another copy.
Although media motivates this design, an object’s payload can also be application data. The transport handles names and delivery. The application and its media format agree on what the delivered bytes mean.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
Why use MoQ?
The obvious way to send a lecture is to send every byte to every viewer. This works while everyone can keep up. But what happens when one student’s connection slows down?
Suppose the lecturer produces four megabits of media each second, but one viewer’s connection can carry only two. Each second adds more work to the queue. Waiting for every byte makes that viewer fall further behind the lecture.
We could drop some old video to catch up, but we have to choose what to drop. Compressed video often stores changes from earlier pictures. The decoder, which turns compressed data back into pictures, needs those earlier pictures to apply the changes. If we drop one at random, we might also lose the pictures that depend on it.
MoQ gives content a structure that the distribution network can use. Objects belong to groups, and a media format can arrange those groups around useful starting points. A relay can recognize the boundaries, reuse objects requested by several viewers, and choose which work to send on each viewer’s connection. It can do this without decoding the pictures. QUIC supplies separate byte streams so that unrelated content need not all wait behind the same missing bytes. See the draft’s motivation and relay model.
Now imagine a student asking the lecturer a question while a thousand others listen. The two people speaking need to hear each other quickly. The listeners might be happier with a little more buffering if it keeps the lecture smooth. We can serve the same publication to both and make different delivery choices along their paths.

Using one protocol along the path
There’s also the work of connecting the pieces. A service might receive the lecturer’s video through one protocol, repackage it for broadcast, and maintain a separate path for conversation. Each boundary needs code and has its own failure modes.
MoQ aims to use the same delivery protocol from publisher through relays to viewers. This is the draft’s convergence goal. It can reduce repackaging between those stages, though viewers still need compatible codecs and media formats. Cloudflare’s MoQ: Refactoring the Internet’s real-time media stack explains why streaming systems often combine several protocols.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
How does MoQ work?
We can follow a publication through five activities:

Connect: establish a compatible session.
Discover: find the publication and its tracks.
Request: choose the content to receive.
Deliver: move objects to the subscriber.
Present: decode and play the media.

We’ll look at each activity in turn. In a running application, some can happen at the same time. If the player already knows the track names, it can skip discovery.

Connect: establish a session
The viewer connects to a server using QUIC or, in the browser path covered here, WebTransport. The endpoints agree on a MOQT version and exchange session settings. They can then request content within that session. QUIC and WebTransport explains the transport; Publishing and Subscribing explains the session.


Discover: find the content
The application turns the viewer’s choice of lecture into names. It may already know the publication or use discovery to find it. A media description then tells the player which tracks contain audio and video and how to interpret them. Tracks, Groups and Objects introduces names, and Media and the Browser explains the media description.


Request: choose what to receive
The viewer subscribes to the tracks it wants, such as audio and low-resolution video. A late arrival may also need earlier objects before playback can begin. The receiver can request retained content while following new objects. Publishing and Subscribing follows acceptance, late joining, and cancellation.


Deliver: forward useful objects
A relay can receive content once and forward it to several viewers. Each viewer has a separate connection, so one may build a queue while another keeps up. Priorities and delivery timeouts help decide which work to send and which to abandon. Relays and Distribution explains the paths; Latency and Congestion explains what happens when they slow down.


Present: turn objects into sound and pictures
The player interprets the media format, decodes the content, and schedules playback. Receiving bytes is only part of that work: the player also needs a usable decoding starting point and timestamps. Media and the Browser follows the path from received objects to the screen and speakers.

title: 1  What, Why and How
section: How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?
text:
How does MoQ compare with WebRTC?
WebRTC and MoQ can both carry a live conversation or a broadcast. They organize the work differently. WebRTC gives a browser an integrated media connection; MOQT gives applications a way to publish and request named content. The practical difference is how much of the media system your chosen stack supplies.

What the browser does for you
For a video call, the browser’s WebRTC stack handles encoding, media transport, receiving, and decoding. The application uses RTCPeerConnection, supplies signaling to exchange setup information, and decides who joins the room. Capturing a microphone and attaching received media to a player still require application code. See the WebRTC API.
With MoQ, a media library handles capture, encoding, decoding, and playback around MOQT’s object delivery. You can use a library that puts these together for you, or build the pieces your application needs. The relay can forward the objects without decoding their media. See the MOQT object model.


How content reaches people
The devices also connect differently. A home router often uses NAT, or Network Address Translation, to let several devices share a public address. A student can connect out, but someone across the Internet can’t simply connect to that student’s private address. Finding a path through this setup is called NAT traversal.
WebRTC handles this with ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment). The browsers exchange possible addresses through the app’s signaling and test which paths work. STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) helps discover the addresses their routers expose. If a direct path works, media can travel between the peers. Otherwise, ICE can select a path through a TURN (Traversal Using Relays around NAT) server. See the ICE introduction and WebRTC’s connectivity requirements.
Our browser MoQ setup connects both participants to a reachable relay instead. WebTransport lets a browser connect to a server, but doesn’t let another browser accept that connection as a peer. MOQT adds no NAT traversal. Both sides open outgoing connections, their routers allow return traffic on those paths, and the relay forwards media between them. That’s why this setup needs the relay even for a two-person call. See moq.dev’s conferencing setup.
For a larger WebRTC call, a selective forwarding unit, or SFU, can receive each participant’s media and forward selected streams to others. This handles distribution, while TURN provides a connection path when direct connectivity fails. WebRTC can therefore use servers for scaling too. See the SFU topology.
MoQ relays distribute requested tracks and can retain objects for later requests. For our lecture, that means a relay can forward the current audio while supplying a newly arrived viewer with earlier video needed to begin decoding. Caching is an explicit part of MOQT’s relay model; retaining enough useful content remains an implementation decision.

To compare the two, look at the whole system: the encoder, servers, player, and network. A WebRTC service can reach a large audience, and a MoQ service can support a conversation. How well either works depends on how you build and run it.


They can work together
The moq.dev project now documents WebRTC import and export gateways, using WHIP and WHEP for HTTP-based WebRTC session setup. A gateway lets a service connect existing WebRTC tools to a MoQ distribution path. Check the gateway’s supported codecs and direction of operation before choosing one.
An existing WebRTC publisher can feed a gateway that publishes the content over MoQ. The gateway has to translate media packaging and session behavior; replacing a socket is not enough. Lorenzo Miniero’s Meetecho interoperability demo shows one such bridge.
For a practical evaluation, start with one complete path: a speaker, a relay or media server, and a viewer on a constrained connection. Measure join time, conversational delay, stalls, and recovery. Then increase the audience. For more on these tradeoffs, read webrtcHacks’ comparison by use case.

title: 1  What, Why and How
text:
The protocol and the project
You will encounter two related names as you read: the IETF MoQ work and the moq.dev project. The IETF, the Internet Engineering Task Force, develops the transport specification through public drafts. moq.dev provides applications and libraries, including a smaller protocol model called moq-lite and a media format called hang.
This book follows MOQT draft-21. The protocol is still being developed, so details can change. We point out when an example uses a moq.dev feature instead of a MOQT rule. If you’re connecting two implementations, check that they agree on the protocol version and media format. The references list the versions and sources used in this edition.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
A short introduction to TCP/IP
Before we look at MoQ messages, let’s look at how their bytes travel. QUIC carries them over a secure connection with several independent byte streams. In a browser, we use WebTransport to work with those streams and with datagrams.
We’ll start with TCP/IP, then see what happens when packets go missing and how QUIC lets us stop sending old content. After that, we’ll look at WebTransport. The packet layouts and handshake are at the end; you can come back to those when you want the details.
If you are already familiar with TCP/IP, TCP, and UDP, skip ahead to Why one ordered stream can hurt.
When a student connects to the lecture, their packets usually pass through several networks. A router forwards each packet toward its destination. IP, the Internet Protocol, provides the addresses and delivery rules that make this possible. An IP address identifies a network interface, such as the one the student is using to connect.
A packet contains a header, which describes how to handle it, and a payload, the data it carries. Layers nest: the payload of an IP packet can contain a UDP datagram, whose payload contains QUIC packets. The receiving software unwraps those layers.
An address gets traffic to a host. A port helps the host direct that traffic to the appropriate transport endpoint. A server may listen for QUIC on UDP port 443 while serving TCP connections on TCP port 443: the transport protocol is part of the distinction. DNS translates a name such as relay.example into addresses the client can try. The client then uses an address to try connecting to the relay.
IP delivery is best effort. Packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or delayed. A full queue in a router is one reason for loss. Each link has a maximum transmission unit, or MTU: its largest IP packet size. The path MTU is the smallest link MTU along the route. Sending one large application message does not make the network carry it as one arbitrarily large packet. See the IPv6 specification for packet-size constraints.

TCP and UDP make different promises
TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, gives an application an ordered byte stream. If bytes go missing, TCP tries to recover them before handing later bytes to the application. The application reads a continuous sequence, even though those bytes traveled in separate packets. Delivery can still fail if the connection breaks.
UDP, the User Datagram Protocol, preserves message boundaries but does not supply ordering or retransmission. The application receives individual datagrams that reach it. A protocol built above UDP can add reliability, security, and congestion control. QUIC does exactly that.

Delay, rate, and feedback
Bandwidth describes a path’s carrying capacity. Throughput is the rate actually achieved. Latency is delay; always name the interval being measured. Network delay and the delay from a camera capturing a picture to a screen displaying it are different measurements.
An acknowledgment, or ACK, tells a sender what transport data arrived. Round-trip time, or RTT, measures a trip to the peer and back. A sender uses feedback to estimate the path and detect possible loss. To find out whether those bytes became a picture, we need to check the player too.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
section: Why one ordered stream can hurt
text:
Why one ordered stream can hurt
Imagine sending camera video and captions through a single ordered byte stream. A packet containing video bytes goes missing. Later caption bytes arrive, but the receiver cannot expose them through that stream until the missing earlier bytes are recovered. This is head-of-line blocking.
For a file, waiting for the missing bytes makes sense: we want the whole file in order. For our lecture, the captions may still be useful while the camera video catches up. Putting both on one stream makes them wait together.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Independent streams
QUIC provides multiple reliable, ordered byte streams within one connection. Loss affecting one stream does not impose that stream’s delivery order on another. A stream still has its own ordering: later bytes in that same stream wait for missing earlier bytes.
A byte stream has no built-in message boundaries. If the publisher writes two objects, the receiver cannot assume two reads will return those two objects. MOQT supplies framing so the receiver can find where each object starts and ends. RFC 9000 §2.2 explains this distinction.
All those streams still share the connection’s bandwidth. If the network gets congested, they have less capacity to share.
QUIC applies flow-control limits to both individual streams and their combined data. A receiver that stops consuming one stream can therefore hold up other streams if the connection-wide limit is exhausted. See RFC 9000 §4.1 and RFC 9002 §7.
MoQ uses these streams to separate content that can be useful on its own. In the next chapter, we’ll see how publishers group that content.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Reliability can have an ending
Sometimes the viewer no longer needs the bytes we’re trying to recover. QUIC lets the sender reset a stream, and lets the receiver ask it to stop. We can use this to give up on old video and spend the connection’s capacity on a newer picture.
Suppose an old camera group is still incomplete when the publisher has a new group with everything needed to start decoding again. We could keep repairing the old group, or cancel it and move on. The application chooses when catching up matters more than seeing every picture.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Where datagrams fit
QUIC’s DATAGRAM extension provides messages that are not retransmitted by QUIC when lost. They share the connection’s security and congestion control. They do not promise arrival or ordering, and their size is constrained by the path and negotiated limits.
QUIC does not split a DATAGRAM frame across packets. If an application’s message is too large, it must choose another mapping or define its own fragmentation and reassembly. That also means deciding what to do when one fragment is missing. See RFC 9221 §5.
That can suit a small, replaceable sensor update. It is less convenient for a large video frame that cannot fit in a datagram. A protocol must define how content maps onto these tools; “uses UDP” alone says very little about reliability.
A QUIC datagram is also different from a UDP packet. QUIC adds its own framing, encryption, and congestion behavior on top of UDP.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Migration and multipath
Suppose a publisher has both cellular and satellite access. It could switch to cellular when satellite service becomes poor, or use both links at once. These are different transport capabilities.
Connection migration lets a QUIC connection move to a new network path while keeping the connection alive, subject to validation and the peer’s migration settings. Base QUIC sends application data on one path at a time. Migration can preserve a session when a device changes networks, though detecting and validating the new path can still interrupt delivery. See RFC 9000 §9.
The multipath extension allows one QUIC connection to use several paths simultaneously. Both endpoints must support and negotiate it. This is separate from the MOQT specification; we refer here to QUIC multipath draft-21, which is still awaiting RFC publication at the time of writing.
Having two links also creates a scheduling decision: which data should use which path? The extension leaves that policy to implementations. A path with spare capacity may have too much delay for an urgent frame. Sending successive parts of a stream over paths with different delays can also make later bytes wait for earlier ones. More capacity alone doesn’t ensure lower playback latency.
An application can instead open separate MoQ connections and decide which one carries each subscription. Those are separate sessions, rather than multiple paths inside one QUIC connection. The moq.dev article On a Boat discusses both approaches. Check the chosen implementation’s support before relying on either in a deployment.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Security belongs to the connection
Running over UDP does not mean sending plaintext. QUIC uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3, the security protocol also used by HTTPS, to authenticate the server and establish keys that protect packets. With a relay in the middle, the publisher-to-relay and relay-to-viewer connections have separate protection. Hiding the content from the relay itself requires another layer, which we will discuss in the security chapter. See RFC 9001 §4.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
WebTransport is the browser doorway
Browser JavaScript does not generally get a raw QUIC socket. WebTransport exposes streams and datagrams to web applications. For the MOQT mapping described in this edition, the browser uses WebTransport over HTTP/3; native software can use QUIC directly.

HTTP/3 is HTTP mapped onto QUIC. Using WebTransport over HTTP/3 does not mean making a new HTTP request for every media object. Once established, the WebTransport session exposes streams and datagrams for the application. See RFC 9114 and the WebTransport API specification.
WebTransport transports application bytes. It does not know that those bytes represent a subscription, an Opus packet, or a camera frame. A MoQ implementation still has to implement the protocol above it.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
A fallback changes the tradeoffs
The moq.dev stack documents a WebSocket fallback. This can help reach networks where the preferred transport is unavailable. It does not preserve all of QUIC’s independent-stream behavior: TCP provides one reliable, ordered byte stream. When the fallback carries all its work over that stream, missing bytes can hold up later bytes belonging to unrelated work.
When testing a player, record which transport it actually used. Otherwise, you can spend a long time explaining “QUIC performance” while measuring a different path.
When the player won’t start, check the connection first, then the MoQ session, then the media. A client might reach the server but speak the wrong protocol version, or receive content its decoder can’t use.

title: 2  QUIC and WebTransport
text:
Reading a QUIC packet
The rest of this chapter looks inside the transport. You can continue to Tracks, Groups and Objects now and return here when you want to read packet fields.
A QUIC frame is a transport instruction inside a QUIC packet. It is unrelated to a video frame, which represents a picture. A packet can carry several QUIC frames, including stream data from different streams.








QUIC frame
What it carries
Why it matters




STREAM
Stream ID, byte offset, and data; optionally an end marker
Places received bytes within the right stream


ACK
Ranges of received packet numbers
Gives the sender delivery feedback


CRYPTO
Cryptographic handshake data
Establishes the connection’s security


MAX_DATA / MAX_STREAM_DATA
Connection / stream flow-control limits
Allows more stream bytes to be sent


RESET_STREAM
An error code and final size for an abandoned sending direction
Ends that direction without delivering every byte


STOP_SENDING
A request to stop a stream’s sending direction
Lets a receiver reject further work


DATAGRAM
An unreliable message, when the extension is negotiated
Carries data without stream ordering or retransmission



For the full frame layouts, see RFC 9000 §19. The DATAGRAM frame is defined in RFC 9221.
Three numbers answer different questions: a packet number identifies a transmission within its packet-number space; a stream ID identifies a stream; a byte offset locates data within that stream. When lost stream data is sent again, it travels in a new packet, with a new packet number. It retains its position in the stream. See RFC 9000 §13.3 for how QUIC retransmits information.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
text:
What is a track?
MoQ names content so that a viewer can request just the pieces it needs. In our lecture, a student joining late might want audio and low-resolution video without downloading the earlier ten minutes.
We’ll build up the names one piece at a time: tracks, groups, then objects. After that, we’ll see how subgroups carry objects on streams and what happens to those names when a publisher restarts.
A track is a named sequence of groups that a subscriber can request. Our lecture has separate tracks for audio, low-resolution video, and high-resolution video. Subscribing to video-low asks for that sequence; it does not also request video-high.
Tracks belong to a namespace, which lets the application organize related names. For this lecture, we use the namespace lectures / session-7. Together, the namespace and track name identify the full track.
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Selecting tracks from a lecture
  accDescr: The lecture namespace contains audio, video-low, and video-high tracks. The example viewer subscribes to audio and video-low.
  L["Namespace: lectures / session-7"] --> A["Track: audio"]
  L --> V["Track: video-low"]
  L --> H["Track: video-high"]
  A --> S["Student receives audio and low-resolution video"]
  V --> S
We’ve written the names as text to make the example easy to follow. MOQT sends namespace components and track names as bytes, so the publisher and subscriber need to use exactly the same bytes. See track naming in draft-21 §2.4.1.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How do groups provide starting points?
text:
How do groups provide starting points?
A group organizes objects within a track. A video format can use each group as a place to begin decoding. That answers the late-arriving student’s next question: where should playback start?
Many compressed pictures describe changes from earlier pictures. Receiving one of these predicted frames without its reference pictures is like receiving “move it two pixels to the left” without knowing what “it” is. A keyframe provides a picture from which decoding can restart.
For our video format, the publisher begins each group with a keyframe, then puts the frames that depend on it in the same group. The student can start with a recent group instead of reconstructing the entire lecture. The player also needs the codec configuration, which the media format supplies separately.





flowchart LR
  accTitle: Two independently decodable video groups
  accDescr: Group 41 starts with its own keyframe and dependent frames. Group 42 starts with a new keyframe and has no picture dependency on group 41 in this example.
  subgraph G41["Group 41"]
    direction TB
    A["Object 0: keyframe"] --> B["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    B --> C["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end
  subgraph G42["Group 42"]
    direction TB
    D["Object 0: new keyframe"] --> E["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    E --> F["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end






Each arrow runs from a reference picture to a picture that needs it. These are decoding dependencies, not network packets. A viewer who has missed group 41 can still use group 42. This is why MOQT recommends independently useful groups. A group boundary alone cannot make a picture decodable: the publisher must put a suitable picture there.
Group IDs order groups within the track. Group 42 does not mean “42 seconds,” and groups need not have equal duration. The media format carries timing information for playback.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
text:
What identifies an object?
Inside each group are objects. Each normal object has an ID and a payload: the bytes being delivered. Our example puts one encoded picture in each object. Other media formats can divide their data differently. Subscription delivery also uses payload-free status markers to signal the end of a group or track; those markers are not encoded pictures. See object status in draft-21 §11.1.2.

Suppose another service also has a track called video-low under lectures / session-7. That’s fine as long as the services belong to different scopes. A scope is the set of servers that agree to treat a full track name as the same track. Within our lecture service’s scope, the full address above must always refer to the same payload. See objects (§2.1) and scope (§2.5).
This property is called immutability. Once published, an object’s payload does not change. If Alice and Bob request the same object, a relay can serve the same stored bytes to both. A corrected payload needs a new identity; otherwise the relay would have no way to know which version the name means.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How do subgroups map objects to streams?
text:
How do subgroups map objects to streams?
A subgroup organizes objects from one group for delivery. It lets the publisher put related objects on the same stream while separating other work.
For subscription delivery, MOQT normally carries each subgroup on one subgroup stream. Within a subgroup, objects are ordered by object ID. This lets the publisher separate work that benefits from separate transport streams. A subgroup can use another stream if an earlier stream was reset prematurely or upstream conditions forced objects out of order; different subgroups must not share a subscription stream.
For example, a layered video codec might produce a base layer that gives a usable picture and an enhancement layer that adds detail. Putting them in separate subgroups lets a scheduler favor the base layer when capacity is scarce. The enhancement still depends on the base; a separate stream does not remove that media dependency.
A subgroup organizes delivery; its ID is not an extra component of the object address in the table above. Objects delivered as datagrams do not belong to subgroups, and fetched objects have their own stream representation. These distinctions are defined in draft-21 §2.2.

Keep the two kinds of structure separate
A track describes content. A stream carries bytes. Their lifetimes need not match: one video track can continue throughout the lecture while new subgroup streams open as new groups are published.

This distinction matters in logs: a subgroup stream ending can be normal even while the track and subscription remain active.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: What happens to names after a restart?
text:
What happens to names after a restart?
Suppose the lecturer’s publisher crashes. When it restarts, it reuses video-low, group 42, object 1 for a new picture. A relay still has the old picture stored under that address. It cannot safely treat both as the same immutable object.
We could put the restarted lecture under a fresh namespace, such as lectures / session-8. Or we could keep track of the group IDs and continue without reusing them. Either way, a new picture needs an address that won’t collide with an old one.
The relay can now distinguish the new content from its cached objects. Next, we’ll follow a student’s request for a track.

title: 3  Tracks, Groups and Objects
section: How does moq-lite name these concepts?
text:
How does moq-lite name these concepts?
When working with the moq-lite implementation, you will encounter broadcast for a named collection of tracks and frame for the payload unit corresponding to an object. moq-lite omits MOQT subgroups and normally sends each group on its own stream. Since moq-lite 05, a small group containing one frame can instead use a datagram, subject to the transport’s size limit. Keep that distinction in mind when moving between its documentation and the IETF specification.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Establishing a session
A subscription asks another endpoint to send objects from a named track. Alice wants to hear the lecture, so her player subscribes to its audio track.
We’ll follow Alice as she connects, finds the lecture, asks for audio, and joins the video partway through. Then we’ll see how she ends a subscription when she leaves.
Alice’s player and the relay first agree on a MoQ session. The session holds the settings and request state they need to exchange content over their transport connection.
In MOQT draft-21, version selection happens during transport establishment. Native QUIC uses ALPN, a handshake field identifying the application protocol; WebTransport uses its protocol negotiation header. The identifier for this edition’s draft is moqt-21. The network can be reachable while session setup fails because the endpoints have no protocol version in common. See §6.2.
Each endpoint opens a control stream and starts it with SETUP, exchanging session options and supported extensions. Each control stream is unidirectional: only the endpoint that opened it sends on it. A request such as SUBSCRIBE uses a separate bidirectional stream, so the other endpoint can answer on that same stream. Objects travel separately from these request messages.
The implementation can overlap some of this work. Requests and data may be sent while initialization is still underway. The draft recommends buffering early arrivals until setup completes, but permits an endpoint to reset early request streams if it cannot support or does not want to buffer them. The endpoint need not wait for a reply at each step before starting the next. See §6.3.

From a connection to the first object

The diagram shows setup first to make it easier to follow; requests and data can also arrive during setup, as described above. The SUBSCRIBE_OK reply accepts the subscription, and the objects travel on separate data streams. See draft-21 §6.4.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Finding the lecture
Before asking for media, the application must turn Alice’s choice into track names. The lecture page might already contain a publication name, or it might use namespace discovery to find available publishers. The application can use discovery results to build a room list or public directory.
Once it finds the publication, the player reads its media description. This tells it which tracks contain audio and which contain video renditions: alternative encodings, such as low-resolution and high-resolution video. Alice’s player can start by choosing audio and a low-resolution rendition. We will examine that media description in the browser chapter.
Discovery and delivery can have different access rules. A private lecture might be hidden from the room list as well as unavailable for playback. Knowing its name does not grant permission to receive it. MOQT provides namespace discovery mechanisms; the service supplies the access policy.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Asking for audio
Alice’s player sends SUBSCRIBE, naming the lecture’s audio track and specifying its delivery choices. The relay answers with SUBSCRIBE_OK if it accepts, or REQUEST_ERROR if it rejects the request. Acceptance establishes the subscription. Audio objects arrive separately from the request and response messages.
What if the relay isn’t receiving the lecture yet? It needs to find the publisher and make its own subscription. The relay can learn where the publisher is from registration, configuration, or discovery. In the example below, the relay already knows where the publisher is, and both subscriptions ask for compatible delivery settings.





sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A viewer subscribes through a relay
    accDescr: Alice subscribes to audio at the relay. The relay obtains an upstream subscription from the publisher, accepts Alice's request, and forwards audio objects.
    participant A as Alice
    participant R as Relay
    participant P as Publisher
    A->>R: SUBSCRIBE audio
    R->>P: SUBSCRIBE audio
    P-->>R: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    R-->>A: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    P->>R: Audio objects
    R->>A: Audio objects






There are now two subscriptions: Alice’s request to the relay, and the relay’s request to the publisher. The relay receives the audio on one connection and forwards it on the other. If it was already receiving the lecture, it could reuse that content instead of asking the publisher again.
Now Bob opens the same lecture and asks for the same audio. The relay can reuse its upstream content while maintaining a separate downstream subscription for Bob. If Alice leaves, Bob still needs that content. If both leave, and no recorder or other consumer remains, the relay can cancel its upstream request. This is how a relay combines demand without making every viewer share one connection. See §7.
The publisher can initiate a subscription too, by offering a track with PUBLISH. The receiver accepts with REQUEST_OK—called PUBLISH_OK when accepting a publication in this draft—or rejects with REQUEST_ERROR. A relay must already know the client is interested in and authorized for that content. Either direction of initiation establishes the same kind of subscription. See §3.1.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Joining video in the middle
Audio is arriving, and Alice’s player also requests video. The publisher is halfway through group 42. In our example, the group’s first object contains a keyframe and the later frames depend on earlier pictures. Receiving only the next new frame may therefore leave Alice with bytes she cannot decode.
The player can retrieve the beginning of group 42 while following new objects, or wait for the next independent group. The first choice can start playback sooner if the missing content is available and quick to deliver. The second avoids catching up through the current group, but waits for a new decoding starting point.
A fetch asks for a bounded portion of a track. In draft-21, the publisher answers a standalone FETCH with FETCH_OK or REQUEST_ERROR. If it accepts, it sends the objects on a separate data stream and ends that stream when delivery is complete. See §3.2.1.
For Alice’s first choice, draft-21 also allows FILL_PARAMETERS on the subscription. These request a bounded fill range on a fetch stream alongside ongoing subscription delivery. The ranges can overlap, so the player must handle duplicate objects; pairing a fill through the largest known object with a subscription starting at the next object avoids that overlap. For the second choice, a location filter can start delivery at the next group. A location is a group ID and object ID: a position in the track, rather than a clock reading. See fill ranges (§3.4) and location filters (§3.3.1).





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Two ways to join a video track
    accDescr: Alice joins during group 42. She can retrieve its earlier objects and follow new ones, or wait for the independently decodable group 43. Either route needs codec configuration before decoding.
    J["Alice joins during group 42"] --> C["Retrieve earlier objects in group 42"]
    J --> W["Wait for group 43"]
    C --> F["Combine with ongoing delivery"]
    W --> K["Receive group 43 from its keyframe"]
    F --> D["Decode with the codec configuration"]
    K --> D






Alice has a wait either way: time to download the start of group 42, or time for the publisher to produce group 43’s keyframe.
Both choices depend on the media format identifying usable starting points. Switching from low-resolution to high-resolution video raises the same question: where can the decoder begin using the new rendition?
Fetching also depends on retention. The relay may have discarded the beginning of group 42, or never received it. To offer a “rewind 30 seconds” button, the service must retain enough content and map playback time to track locations. The player can then translate the requested time into a fetch range.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
Ending a subscription
When Alice disables video, her player should cancel the video subscription while leaving audio active. Otherwise, the relay continues doing work she no longer needs.
In draft-21, cancellation abruptly closes the request stream’s open directions. STOP_SENDING asks the peer to stop its sending direction; RESET_STREAM abandons the cancelling endpoint’s own sending direction. A plain FIN only means that no more bytes will be sent in one direction. A subscriber can finish sending request messages while still expecting content, so FIN alone does not cancel the request. See §6.4.2.2–3.
When the publisher ends an established subscription, it closes the associated data streams, sends PUBLISH_DONE, and closes its request-stream direction. The data streams and request stream can arrive in different orders. Alice may therefore receive PUBLISH_DONE while some final object data is still on its way. See §3.1.1 and §9.9.
Subscription lifetime also matters to authorization. If Alice’s permission expires during the lecture, the service needs a policy for the subscription she already holds, as well as for any new request. Publication permission is separate: allowing Alice to watch must not allow her to replace the lecturer’s content.

title: 4  Publishing and Subscribing
text:
What happens after a disconnect?
If Alice loses the session, opening a new connection is only the first recovery step. Her player needs to establish a new session, make its requests again, and choose a usable place to resume. If the relay still has the missing objects, the player may recover them; if they are gone or too old for live playback, it needs a newer decoding starting point.
A planned shutdown gives the endpoints more time. Draft-21 defines GOAWAY so an endpoint can announce that its session will close; a server can also suggest a new session URI. The client still has to establish the replacement session. See graceful session migration (§6.6.1).

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
text:
How does a relay share content?
A relay receives content from a publisher and forwards it to subscribers. It moves the copying work off the publisher’s connection, allowing the same publication to reach more viewers.
How does one copy from the lecturer become a copy for every student? We’ll follow the relay’s subscriptions, look at what it caches, and see how it handles viewers with different connection speeds. We’ll also look at which jobs need other parts of the service.
The relay subscribes to the lecturer’s content, then publishes it to the students. It has a separate connection on each side and reads the MoQ messages to decide what to forward.

  R --> B["Bob"]

With several interested viewers, a relay can share upstream content and forward it to each downstream connection. If a second relay is closer to another audience, it can repeat that pattern. Viewers in each region can receive content from their local relay.

What happens when one relay is full?
Moving the copies to a server gives us somewhere to add capacity. Suppose our 100 students are split between two regions. We could put a relay in each region and have each receive one copy from an upstream relay. The upstream relay sends two copies, and each regional relay sends 50. The lecturer still sends one.
This is how the distribution tree grows: each relay shares the content coming in and makes copies for the viewers or relays below it. We still pay for those outgoing bytes and connections, but adding viewers no longer means asking the lecturer’s laptop and home connection to carry every copy. The service has to provide enough relay capacity and route viewers to it. See the MOQT relay motivation.


Why does everyone connect to a server?
We need a reachable relay even if there are only two participants behind private networks. In this browser setup, WebTransport connects each client to a server. It doesn’t open a direct browser-to-browser connection, and MOQT adds no NAT traversal. The lecturer and student therefore both connect out to the relay, which carries the media between them. The opening comparison explains how this differs from WebRTC’s ICE, STUN, and TURN setup.
WebRTC can use ICE to test paths between the participants, with STUN to discover addresses and TURN to carry traffic if a direct path fails. That gives a two-person call a chance to avoid a media relay. Our browser MoQ setup connects both participants to the relay from the start.
The relay receives those connections and forwards the requested tracks between them. It doesn’t run a NAT traversal procedure on the clients’ behalf. If the network blocks the chosen transport, the client still needs a supported fallback or another way to reach the server.


Can subscriptions reduce encoding work too?
Suppose the lecturer offers high- and low-resolution video, but every viewer chooses the lower resolution. Forwarding only that track saves network traffic. Avoiding the unused high-resolution encoding can also save work at the publisher.
The moq.dev concepts guide describes how subscriptions carry demand back to the publisher. An application using its library can start an encoder for the first subscriber and stop it after the last one leaves. A recorder counts too, so closing every player may still leave someone receiving the track. The application has to implement this behavior; MOQT doesn’t control the encoder.
The moq.dev article On a Boat gives another example: several cameras share a limited uplink, with higher-resolution tracks requested only when needed. Subscriptions can save bandwidth even with a single viewer.
There’s a startup cost to consider. When the first viewer asks for an idle rendition, the publisher needs to start encoding and send the configuration and a picture the viewer can decode. Until then, that viewer has to wait.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: What does a relay need to know?
text:
What does a relay need to know?
A relay uses names, group boundaries, priorities, and delivery rules. It need not inspect the encoded picture to forward it. The same relay can forward audio, video, and application data.
For this to work, the publisher needs to put the right media at each group boundary. Suppose the relay sends a new viewer a group that depends on pictures from the previous group. The relay has delivered what was requested, but the player still can’t show it.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: How does caching help new viewers?
text:
How does caching help new viewers?
A caching relay can hold recently received objects. A new viewer may obtain a useful group without waiting for the original publisher to send it again. An object is identified by its full track name, group ID, and object ID within a scope. Its payload cannot change, allowing different viewers to reuse the same cached bytes. Some object properties can change under their own rules; immutability does not apply to every cached field.
How much history is available depends on the relay. MOQT allows caching, and each relay decides what to keep within its memory budget. A viewer joining late needs to find out whether the objects it wants are still there.
For the lecture, retaining a few useful recent groups may improve startup. Keeping the entire class for replay is a separate storage feature with different costs and lifetime requirements.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: How does delivery differ between viewers?
text:
How does delivery differ between viewers?
The lecturer’s connection can be fast while one viewer’s connection is slow. A relay has to make downstream delivery decisions for each path. Slowing every viewer to match the slowest one would defeat the point of independent subscriptions.
Alice’s connection may deliver each new group immediately, while Bob’s connection builds a queue. Their playback delay differs even though both request the same publication. The relay can choose delivery settings for each subscription according to that viewer’s path.
A live viewer and a recorder can also have different needs. The viewer may skip an old group to stay near live, while the recorder waits for it. If the publisher or relay retains the objects and spare bandwidth becomes available, the recorder can catch up later. Once those objects have been discarded upstream, a more patient subscriber cannot recover them from that source.
Measure at the edges, then trace through the hops. A healthy publisher-to-relay connection says little about a congested relay-to-viewer connection.

title: 5  Relays and Distribution
section: Which jobs belong to the wider service?
text:
Which jobs belong to the wider service?
Suppose a student needs low-resolution video, but the publisher only sends high resolution. Someone has to create the smaller version. A transcoder does that by decoding and re-encoding the media. The service might run one alongside a relay, which then forwards the resulting objects.
The service also has to choose nearby relays, connect them, and recover when one fails. The moq.dev project includes clustering features to help with this setup.
Before scaling the lecture, draw the actual publisher, relay, and viewer paths. Mark where content is cached and where authorization is checked.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Latency
A video can play smoothly and still be seconds behind the person speaking. For someone watching a lecture, that delay might be acceptable. For someone asking the lecturer a question, it makes the conversation difficult.
Keeping playback close to live takes more than a fast connection. The encoder has to produce media at a rate the network can carry, and the player has to decide how long to wait for missing or delayed content. MoQ gives the sender ways to choose which content to deliver and when to give up on it.
Playback latency is the time between capturing media and presenting it to the viewer. Every stage adds to it: capture, encoding, transmission, buffering, decoding, and display. Data can also wait in queues at the publisher, relay, or receiver.
Network delay is only part of this total. A frame that crosses the network quickly can still spend a long time waiting in the player. Likewise, removing a relay hop will do little for a delay caused mainly by encoding or buffering.
Round-trip time, or RTT, measures how long it takes to send data and receive a response. QUIC uses acknowledgment timing to estimate it. A short RTT helps the sender recover from loss sooner, but it doesn’t tell us how far playback is behind capture. See RFC 9002 §5.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Jitter and buffering
Frames don’t always arrive at evenly spaced intervals. Some take longer than others, and several may arrive together after a delay. This variation in arrival timing is jitter.
The player buffers media so it can present frames at their intended times despite uneven arrivals. More buffered media gives a late frame more time to arrive, but also makes the viewer wait longer. With a smaller buffer, playback stays closer to live but is more likely to run out of media.
There’s no single buffer size that suits every application. A lecture broadcast can tolerate more delay than a conversation with the lecturer. The player has to choose how much delay is acceptable and what to do when a frame misses its playback time.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Bandwidth
The network must carry media as quickly as the publisher produces it. We describe the media’s bitrate in bits per second. For example, 4 Mb/s means four million bits each second, or half a megabyte before packet headers and other overhead.
The capacity available to a connection changes as it shares links with other traffic. A video that fits comfortably at the start of a session may become too large when another device starts a download or the viewer moves to a weaker wireless connection.
Average bitrate also hides bursts. A large keyframe takes more time to send than a small frame, even when the average fits within the available capacity. A queue can absorb a short burst. It cannot absorb a sustained excess without growing.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Congestion
When more traffic reaches a network link than it can forward, packets wait in a queue. As the queue grows, packets take longer to arrive. If the queue fills, packets may be dropped.
Congestion control adjusts the transport’s sending behavior in response to network feedback. QUIC uses acknowledgments to track delivery and detect loss; a congestion controller limits how much data can be in flight. The controller described in RFC 9002 §7 reduces its congestion window when it detects loss or explicit congestion signals. QUIC implementations can use other controllers.
Slowing transmission helps the network, but the publisher may keep producing media at the same rate. That moves the waiting data into a queue at the sender. Unless the application also changes what it sends, playback can keep falling behind.

Datagrams can wait too
Choosing datagrams doesn’t remove network queues. A router can hold a packet for a long time before forwarding it, even if nobody will retransmit it after loss. Excessive queueing like this is called bufferbloat. The viewer can receive most of the media and still be far behind.
QUIC datagrams also share the connection’s congestion controller. When it prevents transmission, the sender must wait or drop the datagram. Skipping retransmission changes how loss is handled; it doesn’t guarantee prompt delivery. See RFC 9221 §5.4.
The moq.dev article Never* use Datagrams explains why timely delivery takes more than allowing packet loss. It argues for using independent streams, prioritizing useful content, and cancelling work that has become too old. Those choices still need congestion control to keep queues from growing.


Flow control
A receiver can also be too slow to consume incoming data. QUIC’s flow control lets it limit how much stream data the sender may send, both per stream and across the connection. This protects the receiver’s buffers. It is separate from congestion control, which responds to conditions on the network path. See RFC 9000 §4.
Neither mechanism knows whether the viewer still wants an old video frame. That decision belongs to the media application.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Media adaptation
To keep up with a slower connection, the application must reduce the amount of media it sends. The publisher can lower its encoding bitrate, or the viewer can request a lower-bitrate rendition. This may mean a smaller picture, fewer frames, or more compression.
Suppose a publisher produces 4 Mb/s while a viewer’s connection carries only 2 Mb/s. Ignoring overhead, each second adds 2 Mb to the sender’s queue. After five seconds, 10 Mb are waiting.
Switching to a 2 Mb/s rendition stops the queue from growing, but the old data is still there. Switching to 1 Mb/s leaves another 1 Mb/s available to clear the backlog, which would take ten seconds. These rates are simplified, but the consequence matters: reducing bitrate doesn’t immediately remove accumulated delay.
If that wait is too long, the sender can abandon old content and deliver a newer decoding starting point. It still needs to reduce the bitrate enough to prevent the queue from filling again.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Priorities
Suppose Alice’s connection can no longer keep up with both audio and video. Sending audio first may let her keep following the lecture while the picture struggles. The scheduler chooses which pending data to send, so it needs to know that audio matters more here.
MOQT expresses these choices through priorities and group ordering. In draft-21, smaller priority numbers mean more urgent work. Its recommended scheduler checks subscriber priority first, then publisher priority. When priorities are equal within a subscription, group ordering helps decide which group goes first. Implementations can use other scheduling algorithms. See §5.1 for the full recommendation.
If we send audio first and it uses all the available capacity, video still has to wait. Priority helps us choose who waits; a timeout lets us decide when waiting has gone on too long. When using a library, check its priority conventions, since moq-lite and MOQT use different rules.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Abandoning old content
Suppose video group 41 remains incomplete while group 42 provides a fresh decoding starting point. Finishing group 41 would preserve older pictures, but sending group 42 may bring Alice closer to the lecturer. Independent groups make that choice possible without requiring every preceding picture.
The sender still has to respect the stream’s structure. A reliable byte stream cannot deliver later bytes past a missing section. To abandon a subgroup’s remaining stream data, MOQT resets that stream. A receiver must then use the media format’s dependencies to decide where decoding can resume.
Draft-21 has two optional timeouts for this. One checks how long an object has waited before entering the transport. The other limits the time to finish delivering a completed subgroup. The examples below use a relay’s clock and a 100 ms limit. See §5.2.

Waiting to enter the transport
The object delivery timeout measures age from when the last byte of an object’s header arrives from upstream. At the original publisher, it starts when the application supplies that header. Before handing the object to the underlying transport, the implementation checks its age.





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Object delivery timeout example
    accDescr: The relay receives the complete object header at zero milliseconds. At 120 milliseconds it checks whether to send the object. The 100 millisecond limit has passed, so it resets a subgroup stream or drops a datagram.
    A["0 ms: header received"] --> B["120 ms: ready to send"]
    B --> C["Age exceeds 100 ms"]
    C --> D["Subgroup: reset stream"]
    C --> E["Datagram: drop it"]






Here the object has already spent too long waiting before transmission. For a subgroup, expiry resets the stream rather than removing a few bytes from its middle. For a datagram, the expired message is dropped.
This check is most effective when the application can still control the queue. If it hands large amounts of data to the transport in advance, expired bytes may already be beyond its reach. Draft-21 therefore recommends minimizing transport buffering and checking expiry before retransmission where the transport interface permits it.


Waiting for delivery to finish
The subgroup delivery timeout starts when the endpoint knows all objects in the subgroup have been published. At a relay, receiving the upstream stream’s FIN provides that information. This timer covers remaining delivery work, including recovery after packet loss.





flowchart TD
    accTitle: Subgroup delivery timeout example
    accDescr: At 50 milliseconds the relay learns the subgroup is complete and starts a 100 millisecond timer. At 150 milliseconds it resets the stream if transport delivery is still incomplete.
    A["50 ms: subgroup complete"] --> B["Start 100 ms timer"]
    B --> C["150 ms: still undelivered?"]
    C -->|Yes| D["Reset stream"]
    C -->|No| E["Delivery finished"]






The transport must reach what the specification calls “all data committed” before the timer expires: its completion state for delivering the data, beyond merely accepting bytes into a send buffer. This concerns transport delivery, not whether the player has decoded or displayed the media. Otherwise, the stream is reset. Unlike the object age check, this timer can expire after the sender has handed all the data to the transport.
For datagrams, the subgroup timeout instead uses the same age check as the object timeout; if both are nonzero, the smaller value applies. Zero disables the corresponding timeout. These rules describe a single hop’s delivery decisions. They do not create a capture-to-display deadline across the whole relay network.


Maximum age in moq-lite
The moq.dev moq-lite guide describes a maximum age relative to the media timeline. Older groups can become unwanted as newer media appears. A network stall by itself does not advance that timeline, and sending a backlog in a burst does not make its media new.
Both publisher and subscriber apply the limit. This matters when viewers share upstream delivery: content still useful to a patient viewer may already be too old for someone speaking in the call. Keep this implementation setting separate from draft-21’s local delivery timers and from a player’s capture-to-display delay.

title: 6  Latency and Congestion
text:
Returning to live playback
After the network recovers, Alice may still be watching frames that reached her earlier. A fresh transport queue does not empty the player’s playback queue. The player needs its own policy for skipping stale decoded frames or moving its presentation clock forward, while respecting audio synchronization and decoding dependencies.
Record when fresh objects arrive and when their content is displayed. If arrival recovers but display stays behind, inspect the player’s queue.
Try briefly reducing available bandwidth, then restoring it. Watch whether playback returns near live, stays behind, or repeatedly changes rendition. Record interruptions as well as average delay. A large keyframe can briefly exceed the path’s capacity even when the average bitrate fits, so the sequence of events matters.
Use a repeatable recorded source for the first experiment. It keeps scene complexity and encoder load stable while you investigate the network response. Once you understand that run, repeat on real devices and networks, where capture, rendering, and additional queues can change the result.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
text:
How does the player interpret a track?
A player turns received objects into sound and pictures. MOQT delivers the objects; the media format and player tell the browser how to interpret, decode, and present them.
We’ll follow a picture from the media description to the screen: choose a track, find a starting picture, decode it, and decide when to display it. Our examples use moq.dev’s hang media format and the browser’s WebCodecs API. We’ll also cover playback permissions and cleaning up when the player stops.
The lecture offers an audio track and two video tracks, one at a lower resolution for slower connections. Track names let the player request them, but names alone do not explain how to use their bytes. The player also needs the codec, decoder configuration, and timing information. A codec defines how pictures or sound are encoded and decoded. A container packages the encoded data with information needed to interpret it, such as timestamps.
MOQT carries application payloads without choosing their media format. Our example uses hang, the media layer in the moq.dev stack. Its catalog.json track describes the available renditions and their decoder configuration. A rendition is an alternative encoding of the content, such as the lecture’s lower-resolution picture. See the hang catalog and container documentation.
Suppose the selected video rendition contains H.264 pictures at 1280 × 720 pixels. Its codec identifier tells the player which decoder it needs. Its codec configuration supplies any required setup, either as initialization data or in-band as the format permits, and its container field tells the player how to find the encoded chunks and their timestamps. With this information, the player can check support on the student’s device and subscribe to a suitable track.
flowchart TD
    accTitle: From a lecture catalog to a displayed picture
    accDescr: The player reads the catalog, selects a supported rendition, receives its media objects, parses encoded chunks and timestamps, decodes pictures, then schedules and displays them.
    A[Read the media catalog] --> B[Choose a supported rendition]
    B --> C[Subscribe and receive objects]
    C --> D[Parse chunks and timestamps]
    D --> E[Decode pictures]
    E --> F[Schedule and display]
    A -. Decoder configuration .-> E
    D -. Media timestamps .-> F
The catalog can change after playback starts. The lecturer might add screen sharing, or a rendition might temporarily become unavailable. The player needs to respond to those updates instead of treating the initial list as permanent.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
text:
What does container parsing actually do?
Let’s look inside one payload. In hang’s legacy container, the first bytes encode a timestamp in microseconds as a variable-length integer. The encoded media comes after it. The player reads the timestamp, strips off that header, and passes the media to the decoder with its timing information. It chooses this parser from the container field in the catalog. See the hang container formats.
For example, mistaking timestamp bytes for H.264 data can produce a decoder failure even when delivery was perfect. This is why parsing has its own step in the diagram.


Four things that are easy to confuse








Term
What it describes
In the lecture




Codec
How media is compressed and reconstructed
H.264 video


Rendition
One encoding offered to the viewer
A 720p version of the lecturer’s camera


MoQ object
An addressed unit delivered by the transport
A payload identified by its track, group, and object IDs


Decoded frame
A picture the decoder has reconstructed
A VideoFrame the player can render



An encoded chunk is compressed media ready to submit to a decoder. The media format tells the player how to extract chunks from MoQ objects. One object might contain one video frame, as in our example, but other formats can package them differently.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
text:
Where can decoding begin?
Video compression often describes how one picture differs from earlier pictures. Such a predicted frame is useful only when the decoder has the reference pictures it needs. A keyframe supplies a fresh decoding starting point in the video model we are using.
This explains the group boundaries from the object-model chapter. The publisher starts a video group with a keyframe, then places dependent frames after it. Our late-arriving student can retrieve the beginning of the current group or wait for the next group. Receiving only the middle of a group may leave the decoder without its references, even though every requested byte arrived correctly.
We can’t create a starting point just by cutting the stream every second. The encoder needs to produce a picture that can start the new group, and the packager needs to put the boundary there. The player also needs the decoder configuration for that picture.
The same issue appears when the student switches to higher resolution. The new rendition has its own decoder state. The player changes configuration as needed and starts at a valid decoding point; it cannot simply feed an arbitrary high-resolution predicted frame into the old sequence.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: How does WebCodecs decode the media?
text:
How does WebCodecs decode the media?
WebCodecs gives JavaScript access to media encoders and decoders. For video, the player checks a configuration with VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported(), applies it with configure(), and submits encoded chunks with decode(). Support depends on the actual codec configuration and device, so the presence of the API alone is insufficient.
The decoder calls the player’s output callback with a VideoFrame. The player then holds that picture until it’s time to display it. Your player or media library handles this queue, the playback clock, and rendering. See the VideoDecoder interface for the API.
Each decoded frame holds resources. After rendering or discarding a frame, the player calls VideoFrame.close() when it no longer needs that frame. Waiting for garbage collection can retain scarce resources and stall decoding. Bounded queues are equally important: if rendering slows down, receiving more frames must not cause unlimited memory growth. See the WebCodecs memory model.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: When should a frame be presented?
text:
When should a frame be presented?
Frames do not necessarily arrive at the spacing at which they were captured. Variable network delay produces jitter. If the player displayed pictures on arrival, that uneven timing would become visible movement on the screen.
Media timestamps tell the player how far apart the frames belong. In the example below, the media timeline and receiver clock start at different points. The table uses milliseconds, while WebCodecs VideoFrame.timestamp uses microseconds. The player needs to account for both the starting points and the units.









Frame
Media timestamp
Arrival on receiver clock
Planned display on receiver clock




A

C

The player chooses receiver time 160 as the moment to display media time zero. It adds each subsequent media timestamp to that anchor. Although B and C arrive only five milliseconds apart, the player displays them 34 milliseconds apart, preserving the media timeline.

Arrival time and presentation time





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Uneven arrivals become evenly scheduled presentation
    accDescr: Frame A arrives at receiver time 100 and is displayed at 160. B arrives at 145 and is displayed at 193. C arrives at 150 and is displayed at 227. Each frame waits until its scheduled display time.
    A["A arrives: 100 ms"] -->|"Wait 60 ms"| D["Display A: 160 ms"]
    B["B arrives: 145 ms"] -->|"Wait 48 ms"| E["Display B: 193 ms"]
    C["C arrives: 150 ms"] -->|"Wait 77 ms"| F["Display C: 227 ms"]






Each arrow spans arrival to display, including any parsing and decoding still needed. The example assumes those steps finish before the planned display time. A frame that arrives on time but finishes decoding late can still miss that time. Arrow lengths are not a time scale.
That first 60 ms wait gives later frames some time to arrive. Now suppose B arrives at 205 ms, after its planned display time of 193 ms. The player can skip it or delay playback. Waiting longer at the start would have made room for B, but it would also have delayed every picture.


Keeping audio and video together
Audio follows the same presentation timeline. An audio sample and a picture intended for media time 67 ms can arrive separately; the player schedules them against a shared clock so the lecturer’s voice stays aligned with their face. Over longer sessions it may also need to correct differences between clocks.
To measure how far behind the lecture we are, we also need to relate the lecturer’s capture clock to the viewer’s clock. The playback timestamps above tell us how to space the frames, but don’t give us that relationship.

title: 7  Media and the Browser
section: What else does a browser player need?
text:
What else does a browser player need?
Even after media arrives, the browser may require a user action before it allows playback. A publisher capturing a camera or microphone needs capture permission; publishing a supplied file does not require access to those devices. See the media capture permission rules. Devices can disappear, tabs can become hidden, and the page must release resources when the session ends.
The moq.dev project provides higher-level player and publisher packages that handle much of this integration. Start with those packages for the first experiment. If playback fails, check each step: did the player find the media description, receive a decodable starting picture, decode it, and display it?
