title: 8  Security and Access
text:
What does the connection protect?
A secure connection protects traffic between its endpoints. A private lecture also needs rules about who may discover, watch, or publish it, and whether the relay operator may read its content.
We’ll start with what the connection protects, then decide who can watch or publish the lecture. After that, we’ll look at hiding the content from the relay, protecting cached objects, and limiting how much work a client can request. We’ll finish by testing those permissions.
QUIC uses TLS to establish packet-protection keys and authenticate the server. When a student’s browser verifies the relay’s certificate, it checks that it reached the expected relay under the applicable trust rules. That check does not identify the student to the relay. Client authentication is a separate choice, as explained in RFC 9001 §4.4.
The lecturer and student each have a connection to the relay. The relay terminates both, so it can read the application payload unless the application adds content encryption.
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Two protected connections through a relay
    accDescr: The lecturer connects securely to a relay, and the relay connects securely to the student. These are separate connections. The relay can read the media unless the application encrypts the content end to end.
    P[Lecturer] <-->|Protected connection A| R[Relay]
    R <-->|Protected connection B| S[Student]
For a service that trusts its relay operator with the lecture, this may be the intended arrangement. The transport protects traffic between endpoints, while the relay enforces access rules. If certificate verification fails, check the hostname, certificate, and client trust configuration. Disabling verification would let the client connect without authenticating the server.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: Who may discover, subscribe, or publish?
text:
Who may discover, subscribe, or publish?
Before the relay accepts a request, it needs to answer two questions: who is asking, and are they allowed to do this? Identifying the caller is authentication. Checking their permission is authorization. A student might be allowed to watch the lecture while only the lecturer can publish it.
First, write down the intended access policy. For example, this class might use:









Participant
Discover the class
Subscribe to media
Publish media




Lecturer
Yes
Yes
Yes


Enrolled student
Yes
Yes
No


Visitor
No
No
No



The lecture service sets these permissions. To check that they work, try each action with each kind of account.
Should someone outside the class even see its title in a room list? For a private lecture, the service may need to restrict discovery as well as playback.
The application can put permissions in a credential, such as a JSON Web Token (JWT) if the implementation supports it. Before trusting its claims, the relay must verify the token’s signature or other cryptographic protection with a trusted key and an allowed algorithm. It then checks who issued it, which service it’s for, whether it has expired, and which names and actions it allows. Reading a token’s fields is not the same as validating it. RFC 8725 covers JWT validation, including issuer and audience checks.
A stolen bearer credential can also be reused while it remains valid. Expiration limits when the credential can be accepted, but the service must also decide when to end subscriptions it previously authorized. Test revocation during playback as well as rejection of new requests. MOQT discusses this replay problem in draft-21 §15.3.2.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How can content stay private from the relay?
text:
How can content stay private from the relay?
What if we don’t want the relay operator to be able to watch the lecture either? The lecturer can encrypt the media before sending it, and the students can decrypt it after receiving it. This is end-to-end content encryption.





flowchart LR
    accTitle: Content encryption across an intermediate relay
    accDescr: The lecturer encrypts media with content keys. The relay forwards the encrypted payload using visible routing metadata. An authorized student decrypts the media with the required content keys.
    P[Lecturer encrypts media] --> R[Relay forwards encrypted payload]
    R --> S[Student decrypts media]
    N[Names and delivery metadata remain visible] -.-> R






The service must distribute keys to authorized students, authenticate the content, decide when to change keys, and define how a newly enrolled student joins. These are part of the content-encryption design; establishing QUIC connections does not supply them automatically. MOQT leaves such mechanisms outside the transport specification. See draft-21 §15.4.
The relay can still see enough metadata to forward the content. That may include names, sizes, timing, and who subscribes to whom. So even with encrypted media, think about what those details reveal about a private class.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: Who may publish under a cached name?
text:
Who may publish under a cached name?
The relay may retain objects so that another student can join quickly. This works because an object identity refers to the same payload wherever it is served within the service’s scope. If an attacker could publish different bytes under the lecturer’s identity, those bytes might reach several students through the cache.
The relay needs to check that a publisher owns the names it wants to use, as required by draft-21 §15.3.3. A legitimate publisher also needs to avoid reusing old object addresses after a restart. As we saw in the content-model chapter, it can use a fresh namespace or continue with group IDs that won’t collide with the cache.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How much work may a client request?
text:
How much work may a client request?
Even an enrolled student can ask for more than the server can handle. A client might subscribe to every rendition, repeatedly ask for discovery results, or leave streams stalled. Set limits on connections, subscriptions, queued bytes, and cached content to keep that work manageable.
Consider a low-priority video stream waiting while more urgent audio keeps arriving. Its bytes still occupy memory. In MOQT draft-21, each endpoint, whether publisher or subscriber, must cancel a stream when it reaches a resource limit, preferably its lowest-priority stream. The actual memory budget remains an implementation decision. See §15.5.
For the lecture service, a limit on concurrent track subscriptions can prevent one viewer from requesting every rendition while displaying only one. Monitoring those limits helps distinguish a slow student connection from an application that is creating more work than intended.

title: 8  Security and Access
section: How do we test the access policy?
text:
How do we test the access policy?
A successful playback test checks only the enrolled student’s path. Test the other roles too: a viewer attempting to publish, a student from another class attempting to subscribe, and a client beginning a request with an expired credential. Confirm that each fails at the intended boundary. Keep credentials out of copied logs and shared URLs wherever the integration permits.
For experiments, the moq.dev public anonymous relay is explicitly public and discoverable. Use public test content there. A private lecture needs a relay with deliberate access configuration, followed by the rejection tests above. The project’s development guide describes the public relay, and its production guide covers deployment access configuration.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Find a starting point
You can try MoQ in a browser, run a relay yourself, or build a publisher and subscriber with a transport library. The MoQ Alliance getting-started guide brings these options together, with links to demos, media tools, and implementations in several languages.
Start with something small: one publisher, one relay, and one viewer. Once media is playing, add another viewer and see how the relay shares the publication.
The Alliance guide is a useful place to choose a project based on what you want to build:
For a complete media demo, moq.dev’s setup guide is one option. For other implementations, browse the Alliance’s open-source repository list. Use the chosen project’s documentation for installation commands and supported features.
Before combining projects, check their protocol revision and media format. Two libraries can both implement MoQ and still disagree on the messages or payloads they expect. Record the versions you use so you can reproduce your setup later.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Try live video. Follow its browser demo links to publish in one tab and watch in another.
Run your own relay. Look at the linked relay projects and follow their setup guides.
Use an existing media source. Explore the tools for connecting native media pipelines to MoQ.
Send application data. Look at the transport libraries if your objects contain messages or state rather than audio and video.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Follow the media
A source produces media. An encoder compresses it. The media format supplies timing and decoder configuration, and the publisher makes the content available as tracks. The relay forwards requested objects to the viewer, which decodes and presents them.
Your applicationRooms, permissions, playback decisionsMedia formatCodec configuration, timestamps, payloadsMoQ transportNames, subscriptions, groups, objectsQUIC / WebTransportSecure streams, datagrams, congestion controlThe publisher and player need to agree on both transport and media format.
Use the project’s sample media first if it provides any. That gives you a known source while you get the connection and player working. Then try your camera or another live source.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Add another viewer
Open a second player for the same publication. Both viewers should receive the content, and closing one should leave the other playing. If the relay exposes traffic metrics, compare its upstream and downstream traffic as viewers join.
Try joining after the publisher has been running for a while too. The new viewer needs decoder configuration and a suitable starting point in the media. Watch how long it takes to show the first picture.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Change the network
Reduce the bandwidth available to one viewer, then restore it. Watch whether the player lowers its video quality, pauses, or falls behind. When the connection recovers, does playback return near live?
Use a network test tool that affects the connection you’re using. Browser HTTP throttling may not affect WebTransport traffic. Change one condition at a time so you can tell what caused the result.
You can also briefly disconnect a viewer. Check whether it reconnects on its own and whether it resumes with fresh media or plays through older content first.

title: 9  Your First MoQ System
text:
Run it outside your machine
Follow your chosen implementation’s deployment guide for certificates, network access, and relay configuration. A local demo may allow anonymous publishing and viewing. Before using private content, configure who can publish and subscribe, then test those permissions. The Security and Access chapter explains the decisions involved.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Authentication and authorization
Looking for a term? Related terms are grouped under alphabetical headings, with links back to the chapters that explain them.
Some words, such as “stream,” mean different things depending on whether we’re talking about media or transport. The definitions below follow how we use them in this book.
Authentication: establishing which identity an endpoint or user has.
Authorization: deciding what that identity may do, such as publishing a lecture or subscribing to it.
End-to-end encryption: content protection whose keys are held by the intended content endpoints, so an intermediate relay cannot read the protected payload. Routing metadata can remain visible.
Read more in Security and Access.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Broadcast and catalog
Broadcast: moq.dev’s name for a collection of tracks in one publication, such as the lecture’s audio and video.
Catalog: media metadata describing the available tracks or renditions and how to decode them. The format and schema depend on the media layer in use.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Codec, container, and timestamp
Codec: a method for encoding and decoding media. The codec compresses pictures or sound; the transport delivers the resulting bytes.
Container: a framing format that packages encoded media with information needed to interpret it, such as timestamps. It is distinct from the codec.
Timestamp: a position on a media timeline. It is not automatically a wall-clock time or a measurement of network delay.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Connection and session
Connection: the transport carrying data between two endpoints. In our lecture, the publisher connects to the relay, and the viewer has another connection to that relay.
Session: the MoQ exchange running over that transport. The endpoints agree on a protocol version and settings so they can send requests and content.
Read more in QUIC and WebTransport.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
IP, TCP, UDP, and QUIC
IP: the Internet Protocol, which addresses packets and supports forwarding between networks.
TCP: a transport providing a reliable, ordered byte stream in each direction of a connection.
UDP: a transport carrying separate datagrams without built-in retransmission or ordering.
QUIC: a secure transport over UDP with multiple ordered byte streams and connection-level congestion control.
Packet: a network transmission unit. Packet boundaries do not define MoQ object boundaries.
ACK: an acknowledgment telling the sender which transport data arrived. The player handles decoding and playback separately.
RTT: round-trip time, a measure of network delay to a peer and back.
Read the networking introduction and comparison tables.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Keyframe and rendition
Keyframe: in this guide’s simplified video examples, a picture providing a fresh decoding starting point. Exact random-access behavior depends on the codec and packaging.
Rendition: another encoding of the same content, such as a lower-resolution video. Switching renditions may require new decoder configuration and a new starting picture.
Read more in Media and the Browser.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Latency, jitter, and congestion
Latency: delay between specified events. Always ask which events: packet send and receipt, capture and display, or another pair.
Jitter: variation in delay. A playback buffer can absorb some variation at the cost of additional latency.
Congestion: a condition where demand exceeds available network capacity, causing queues or loss. Application queues can also grow when production outpaces delivery.
Read more in Latency and Congestion.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
MOQT, moq-lite, and hang
MOQT: Media over QUIC Transport, the IETF publish/subscribe protocol described by a versioned draft in this edition.
moq-lite: the smaller protocol model used by the moq.dev project, with implementation-specific compatibility support.
hang: the moq.dev media layer providing catalog and container conventions above its generic transport model.
Read more in What, Why, and How.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Object, group, and subgroup
Object: an addressed unit in MOQT, identified by its full track name, group ID, and object ID within a scope. Normal objects carry application payloads; subscription delivery also uses payload-free end markers. An object is not necessarily a video frame.
Group: a collection of objects within a track. A media format can arrange groups as independent join points; the group boundary alone does not guarantee that the contained media can be decoded.
Subgroup: a delivery grouping of objects within one group, sent in ascending object-ID order on its subgroup stream. Stream-based subscription delivery carries a subgroup on a subgroup stream; FETCH uses its own stream representation. This is part of MOQT’s model and is omitted from moq-lite’s simpler model.
Read more in Tracks, Groups, and Objects.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Publisher, subscriber, and relay
Publisher: an endpoint that supplies requested objects. An original publisher first introduces the content.
Subscriber: an endpoint requesting and receiving a track.
Relay: an intermediary acting as subscriber upstream and publisher downstream. It forwards content and may cache objects.
Read more in Relays and Distribution.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Stream and datagram
Stream: here, usually a reliable ordered QUIC or WebTransport byte stream. A “live stream” in everyday speech is a different concept.
Datagram: an independently delivered message without QUIC retransmission on loss. It does not promise arrival or order and has a size limit.
Read more in QUIC and WebTransport.

title: 10  Glossary
text:
Track and namespace
Track: the named sequence of groups a subscriber can request. Audio and each video rendition can use separate tracks.
Namespace: a tuple of byte sequences that, together with a track name, identifies a track. Slashes in this book make example components readable; they are not the wire encoding.
Scope: the set of servers within which a full track name identifies the same track.
Read more in Publishing and Subscribing.

The protocol baseline
This edition follows Media over QUIC Transport, draft-21, published September 8, 2026. The chapter links use that version. You can find newer revisions on the document status page and follow the wider work through the MoQ working group.
Read the object model before the wire-message tables. You’ll then know what the track, group, and object identifiers refer to when you encounter them in a message.

A route through the MOQT specification
Start with the question you are trying to answer. These links all refer to draft-21, so their terminology and section numbers belong to the same edition.



Question
Where to read




What identifies a piece of content?
Objects (§2.1) and track naming (§2.4.1)

Subscriptions (§3.1), fetch (§3.2), and joining an ongoing track (§3.5)

Read the explanatory sections first, then use control messages (§9) when you need field layouts. The words MUST, SHOULD, and MAY express requirement levels when a specification adopts BCP 14, which comprises RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. In particular, a recommendation is not a guarantee that every implementation will behave identically.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
The transport underneath
RFC 9000 defines QUIC’s transport, including streams, flow control, and cancellation. RFC 9001 describes its use of TLS. RFC 9002 covers loss detection and congestion control.
RFC 9221 defines the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. Read it when deciding whether a small payload should be retried or replaced, and when checking message-size constraints.
QUIC multipath draft-21 describes using several network paths within one connection. It is a separate extension from MOQT. Its publication status was checked on September 23, 2026; it was in the RFC Editor queue.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
Browser interfaces
The W3C WebTransport specification describes the browser API for streams and datagrams. Its presence does not remove the need for a protocol library above it.
The W3C WebCodecs specification describes low-level codec interfaces. It explains how to configure a decoder and release frames when you’re done with them. Playback scheduling still belongs to the player.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
The WebRTC comparison
The early comparison uses the W3C WebRTC specification for the browser interface. The network behavior comes from IETF documents: RFC 8835, section 3.4 covers connection establishment with ICE and relay support, while section 3.5 identifies the media and data transports.
For media, WebRTC uses SRTP, the secure form of the Real-time Transport Protocol. Data channels use SCTP, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol, carried inside DTLS, Datagram Transport Layer Security. You do not need to learn these packet formats to understand the comparison; the distinction is that WebRTC specifies how these pieces fit together for real-time communication.
RFC 7667, section 3.7 explains how a media server can forward selected streams in a WebRTC conference.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
Architectural background
Cloudflare’s MoQ: Refactoring the Internet’s real-time media stack (August 2025), by Mike English and Renan Dincer, explains why streaming systems combine different protocols, then describes MoQ’s layers and follows content through a relay network.
Its implementation discussion targets draft-07, and its message names and scheduling examples predate this book’s draft-21 baseline. Use the pinned draft for those details.

Finding an implementation
The MoQ Alliance’s Get started with MoQ guide collects browser demos, native media tools, and transport libraries in several languages. Use it to choose a starting point for your own system. Follow each project’s own documentation for setup and compatibility; the directory includes implementations targeting different draft revisions.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
Editorial approach and limitations
The initial protocol review was on September 16, 2026. Technical explanations and setup links were checked again on September 22, 2026. Protocol details refer to draft-21, and examples using moq.dev features say so.
The latency numbers in this book are examples, not measurements. We haven’t tested every linked demo or browser. Try your chosen software on the devices and networks you plan to support.

title: 11  References and Reading
text:
Keeping an edition accurate
When updating the book, record the new research date and protocol revision together. Review terminology, setup, subscription behavior, timeout semantics, and the media-format boundary before changing the edition badge.
Keep examples identified as examples. If you add benchmarks, publish the workload, hardware, network conditions, implementation versions, and measurement points. If you add runnable SDK code, pin dependencies and verify it against the corresponding relay. State what you tested and what the results showed.
